newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Yeltsin backs govt reforms, deals with NATO fears.
newsitem.headline: Yeltsin backs govt reforms, deals with NATO fears.

text.p: President Boris Yeltsin approved his reformist government's economic programme on Monday, despite warnings it will be tough on ordinary Russians, and tried to defuse communist opposition to a security pact with NATO.

Yeltsin also named Agriculture Minister Viktor Khlystun as a deputy prime minister in the latest stage of a gradual reshuffle, giving Russia's bloated, beleaguered farm lobby a senior voice in the cabinet.

The president enthusiastically supported the government's short-term economic plan at a meeting with Prime Minister Viktor Chernomyrdin, First Deputy Premiers Anatoly Chubais and Boris Nemtsov and Deputy Prime Minister Oleg Sysuyev.

"This is not a declaration, not just statistics, but rather a business document which addresses every problem facing each Russian and the country as a whole," Interfax news agency quoted Yeltsin as saying.

The seven-point plan contained no new policies but confirmed a trend towards deeper market reforms. It outlined the aims of the cabinet which two months ago replaced a more conservative team that failed to end huge wage and pension arrears.
Chernomyrdin made paying these debts to public sector workers his top priority and pledged to target help to those who really need it -- meaning cutting and restructuring subsidies.

He also vowed to secure an increase in industrial output, revive agriculture through cheap credits, support local initiatives from the centre, cut away at the roots of corruption and teach the state to live honestly, within its means.
"These policies are tough but essential for all our citizens," Chernomyrdin told a news conference.
Yeltsin added the seventh point -- committing the government to more openness and obliging it to explain all its moves.

The government will face a major test when Chernomyrdin and Chubais brief the communist-led State Duma, the lower house of parliament, on Wednesday on the economy and on a plan to cut spending by a fifth because of poor tax revenues.
The communists have made clear they will oppose the plan when it is put to the vote on Friday but Chernomyrdin hoped a compromise could be reached eventually.
"We hope the sequester will be passed. Probably it will not be (passed) immediately but there are things to work on," Chernomyrdin said, promising to work closely with the Duma.

In a separate move, the Kremlin said Yeltsin had issued a decree making Khlystun the seventh deputy prime minister. Khlystun has said he will shake up the agriculture sector but faces a huge task in helping farms adapt to market conditions.
Turning to international matters, Yeltsin briefed the speakers and party chiefs of both houses of parliament on last week's partnership deal between Russia and NATO.

The deal clears the way for Moscow and its former Cold War adversary to sign an agreement in Paris on May 27, mapping out a new relationship and addressing Moscow's concerns over a NATO plan to offer membership to countries in eastern Europe.

Yeltsin said he would review ties with NATO if the alliance ignored Russia's views. "If NATO begins to take decisions without taking account of Russia's opinion, Russia will review its relations with the alliance," he said.
Yeltsin's comments were clearly intended to appease communists and nationalists who oppose the agreement, although he does not need parliamentary approval for the pact.

Interfax said Yeltsin had sent a letter to Ukrainian President Leonid Kuchma in which he explained that Kiev's security concerns had been taken into consideration during negotiations with the Western defence alliance.

A Ukrainian foreign ministry spokesman said Yeltsin was expected to visit Kiev on May 30 and 31 to sign a post-Soviet political deal. Yeltsin has declined until now to visit because of political disagreements.
